# Question 3: Dimension Reduction with PCA {#sec-pca}

Question 2 described each household with six purchase behaviour variables. **Principal component analysis (PCA)** asks whether those six can be summarised by fewer new variables, called components, without losing much information. Each component is a weighted combination of the six: the first captures as much of the variation between households as possible, the second captures as much of what is left as possible while being uncorrelated with the first, and so on. If the six variables overlap, a few components carry most of the information, which makes the households easier to describe and to plot.

## Is PCA worth doing on these variables?

PCA can only compress variables that move together. If the six were unrelated, every component would carry about the same share and nothing would be gained.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-pca-correlation
#| tbl-cap: "Correlations between the six prepared variables (the same data the clustering used)."

pca_cor <- soap_prep |>
  select(all_of(cluster_vars)) |>
  cor()

# The strongest pair, and each variable's largest correlation with any other
top_pair <- as_tibble(pca_cor, rownames = "var1") |>
  pivot_longer(-var1, names_to = "var2", values_to = "r") |>
  filter(var1 < var2) |>                       # each pair once, no diagonal
  slice_max(abs(r), n = 1)

loner <- as_tibble(pca_cor, rownames = "variable") |>
  pivot_longer(-variable, names_to = "other", values_to = "r") |>
  filter(variable != other) |>
  group_by(variable) |>
  summarise(max_abs_r = max(abs(r))) |>
  slice_min(max_abs_r, n = 1)

as_tibble(pca_cor, rownames = "variable") |>
  gt() |>
  fmt_number(-variable, decimals = 2) |>
  data_color(columns = -variable, palette = c(pal[4], "white", pal[1]), domain = c(-1, 1))
```

The strongest relationship is between `r top_pair$var1` and `r top_pair$var2` (r = `r round(top_pair$r, 2)`), so there is real overlap for PCA to use. At the other extreme, `r loner$variable` is almost independent of the rest (its largest correlation with any other variable is `r round(loner$max_abs_r, 2)`), so it cannot be folded into the others and is likely to need a component of its own.

## Running the PCA

The PCA follows the tidymodels pattern from the Week 7 tutorial: a recipe with `step_normalize()` and `step_pca()`, estimated with `prep()`, and checked against base R's `prcomp()`.

```{r}
#| label: pca-fit

pca_data <- soap_prep |> select(MemberID, all_of(cluster_vars))

pca_rec <- recipe(~ ., data = pca_data) |>
  update_role(MemberID, new_role = "id") |>       # keep the ID, but leave it out of the PCA
  step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors()) |>     # see the note below
  step_pca(all_numeric_predictors(), num_comp = length(cluster_vars), id = "pca") |>  # keep all six for now
  prep()

# What step_normalize learned: for already standardised data, means are 0 and sds are 1
norm_check <- tidy(pca_rec, number = 1) |>
  group_by(statistic) |>
  summarise(furthest = max(abs(value - if_else(statistic == "mean", 0, 1))))

# Cross-check against base R: prcomp() should give the same variances
pca_base <- prcomp(select(pca_data, all_of(cluster_vars)))
```

**Is `step_normalize()` needed again?** PCA must be run on standardised data, otherwise the variable with the largest units (volume) would dominate the first component only because its numbers are bigger. `soap_prep` was already standardised in @sec-prep, so this step changes nothing here: the means it learned differ from 0, and the standard deviations from 1, by at most `r signif(max(norm_check$furthest), 1)`, which is rounding error. It is kept so that the recipe is safe on its own if it is ever run on unprepared data. All six components are kept at this stage so that the number to retain is chosen from the evidence below rather than fixed in advance.

## How many components to keep

```{r}
#| label: tbl-pca-variance
#| tbl-cap: "Variance explained by each component."

pca_var <- tidy(pca_rec, id = "pca", type = "variance") |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = terms, values_from = value) |>
  transmute(component,
            eigenvalue = variance,
            percent    = `percent variance`,
            cumulative = `cumulative percent variance`)

# The variances match base R's prcomp() (eigenvalue = sd squared)
same_as_prcomp <- isTRUE(all.equal(pca_var$eigenvalue, pca_base$sdev^2, check.attributes = FALSE))

pca_var |>
  gt() |>
  fmt_number(eigenvalue, decimals = 3) |>
  fmt_number(c(percent, cumulative), decimals = 1, pattern = "{x}%") |>
  cols_label(component = "Component", eigenvalue = "Eigenvalue",
             percent = "Variance explained", cumulative = "Cumulative")
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-pca-scree
#| fig-cap: "Left: scree plot with the eigenvalue of 1 marked. Right: cumulative variance with the 70% line."
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4

n_kaiser <- sum(pca_var$eigenvalue > 1)                 # Kaiser: eigenvalue above 1
n_70     <- which(pca_var$cumulative >= 70)[1]          # enough components for 70% of the variation
n_keep   <- n_70                                        # the decision (explained below)

scree <- pca_var |>
  ggplot(aes(component, eigenvalue)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed", colour = pal[6]) +
  geom_line(colour = pal[1]) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = component <= n_keep), size = 3, show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = pal[1], `FALSE` = pal[6])) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = pca_var$component) +
  labs(title = "Scree plot", x = "Component", y = "Eigenvalue")

cumul <- pca_var |>
  ggplot(aes(component, cumulative / 100)) +
  geom_col(aes(fill = component <= n_keep), show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.7, linetype = "dashed", colour = pal[6]) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = pal[1], `FALSE` = pal[6])) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = pca_var$component) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent) +
  labs(title = "Cumulative variance explained", x = "Component", y = NULL)

scree + cumul
```

```{r}
#| label: pca-keep-values
#| echo: false

eig      <- pca_var$eigenvalue
cum_keep <- pca_var$cumulative[n_keep]
```

The first component explains `r round(pca_var$percent[1], 1)`% of the variation on its own, and each further component adds less. Three rules were read together to decide how many to keep:

1. **Kaiser rule** [@kaiser1960] (keep components with an eigenvalue above 1, meaning the component carries more information than a single standardised variable): `r n_kaiser` components.
2. **Share of variance** (keep enough components to explain at least 70% of the variation): `r n_70` components, together explaining `r round(cum_keep, 1)`%.
3. **Scree plot** (keep the components before the curve flattens): after component `r n_keep` the eigenvalues drop to `r round(eig[n_keep + 1], 2)` and `r round(eig[n_keep + 2], 2)`, which are almost level, so the curve flattens there.

**The three rules agree, so `r n_keep` components are retained**, keeping `r round(cum_keep, 1)`% of the information while reducing six variables to three dimensions. One caution: the third eigenvalue is `r round(eig[3], 3)`, only just above 1, so the Kaiser rule alone would be a weak reason to keep it; the share of variance and the scree plot are what make the case. As a check, base R's `prcomp()` gives `r if (same_as_prcomp) "exactly the same eigenvalues" else "different eigenvalues, which needs checking"`.

## Naming and describing the components

The **loadings** are the weights each original variable gets in a component. A loading far from 0 (here beyond ±0.4, a common cut-off) means the variable helps define that component, and its sign says whether the variable rises or falls as the component score rises. The sign of a whole component is arbitrary in PCA (multiplying every loading by -1 describes the same component), so each component is flipped, where needed, so that its largest loading is positive and "a high score" reads naturally.

```{r}
#| label: fig-pca-loadings
#| fig-cap: "Loadings of the three retained components. Dark bars are beyond plus or minus 0.4 and define the component."
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4

kept_pcs <- paste0("PC", seq_len(n_keep))

pca_load_raw <- tidy(pca_rec, id = "pca", type = "coef") |>
  filter(component %in% kept_pcs) |>
  select(variable = terms, component, value)

# Flip each component so its largest loading is positive (direction only, the PCA is unchanged)
pc_flip <- pca_load_raw |>
  group_by(component) |>
  slice_max(abs(value), n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  ungroup() |>
  transmute(component, flip = sign(value))

pca_load <- pca_load_raw |>
  left_join(pc_flip, by = "component") |>
  mutate(value  = value * flip,
         strong = abs(value) >= 0.4)

pca_load |>
  ggplot(aes(value, fct_rev(factor(variable, levels = cluster_vars)), fill = strong)) +
  geom_col() +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(-0.4, 0.4), linetype = "dashed", colour = pal[6]) +
  facet_wrap(~ factor(component, levels = kept_pcs)) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = pal[1], `FALSE` = pal[6]),
                    labels = c(`TRUE` = "Defines the component", `FALSE` = "Weak")) +
  labs(title = "Loadings of the retained components", x = "Loading", y = NULL, fill = NULL)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-pca-loadings
#| tbl-cap: "Loadings of the retained components (bold: beyond plus or minus 0.4)."

pca_load_wide <- pca_load |>
  select(variable, component, value) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = component, values_from = value) |>
  arrange(factor(variable, levels = cluster_vars))

load_gt <- pca_load_wide |>
  gt() |>
  fmt_number(all_of(kept_pcs), decimals = 2) |>
  cols_label(variable = "Variable")

# Bold the loadings that define each component
for (pc in kept_pcs) {
  load_gt <- load_gt |>
    tab_style(style = cell_text(weight = "bold", color = pal[1]),
              locations = cells_body(columns = all_of(pc),
                                     rows = which(abs(pca_load_wide[[pc]]) >= 0.4)))
}
load_gt
```

```{r}
#| label: pca-load-values
#| echo: false

ld <- \(v, pc) sprintf("%+.2f", pca_load_wide[[pc]][pca_load_wide$variable == v])
pv <- \(pc) round(pca_var$percent[pca_var$component == as.integer(sub("PC", "", pc))], 1)
```

**PC1: Shopping activity and brand variety** (`r pv("PC1")`% of the variation). It is defined by NoTrans (`r ld("NoTrans", "PC1")`), NoBrands (`r ld("NoBrands", "PC1")`) and TotalVol (`r ld("TotalVol", "PC1")`), so a high PC1 score means a household that buys often, buys a lot and spreads its purchases across many brands, while a low score is a light, occasional buyer. Because the number of brands loads together with the activity variables, buying more goes with trying more brands: in these data the heaviest buyers are not the most loyal ones (MaxBrShare loads `r ld("MaxBrShare", "PC1")`).

**PC2: Loyal bulk buying versus promotion seeking** (`r pv("PC2")`% of the variation). It is defined by MaxBrShare (`r ld("MaxBrShare", "PC2")`) and TotalVol (`r ld("TotalVol", "PC2")`) against PurPromo6 (`r ld("PurPromo6", "PC2")`). A high PC2 score means a household that puts most of its volume on one brand and buys in quantity without needing a deal; a low score means a household whose purchases lean on promotion 6. This is the loyalty versus deal-seeking axis in the Key Problem, and it is a different idea from how active a household is (PC1).

**PC3: Response to other promotions** (`r pv("PC3")`% of the variation). It is almost entirely PurOtherPromo (`r ld("PurOtherPromo", "PC3")`), the variable that was barely related to any other. It earns a component of its own because this kind of promotion response is separate from both activity and loyalty: knowing how much a household buys, or how loyal it is, says little about whether it takes up these offers.

## The households on the components

Each household gets a score on every retained component. Plotting the first two scores shows the households in two dimensions instead of six, coloured by their segment from Question 2, with the loadings drawn as arrows pointing in the direction in which each variable increases.

```{r}
#| label: fig-pca-biplot
#| fig-cap: "Households on the first two components, coloured by segment. Arrows show the loadings (stretched to be visible; only direction and relative length matter)."
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 6.5

# Component scores, flipped the same way as the loadings, joined to the segments
pca_scores <- bake(pca_rec, new_data = NULL) |>
  select(MemberID, all_of(kept_pcs)) |>
  mutate(across(all_of(kept_pcs), \(x) x * pc_flip$flip[pc_flip$component == cur_column()])) |>
  left_join(soap_clusters |> select(MemberID, segment), by = "MemberID") |>
  mutate(segment = factor(segment, levels = segment_names))

# Arrows: the PC1 and PC2 loadings, stretched so they are visible next to the scores
arrow_scale <- 0.8 * max(abs(c(pca_scores$PC1, pca_scores$PC2)))
pca_arrows  <- pca_load |>
  filter(component %in% c("PC1", "PC2")) |>
  select(variable, component, value) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = component, values_from = value) |>
  mutate(across(c(PC1, PC2), \(x) x * arrow_scale))

ggplot(pca_scores, aes(PC1, PC2)) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = segment), alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_segment(data = pca_arrows, aes(x = 0, y = 0, xend = PC1, yend = PC2),
               arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.2, "cm")), colour = "black") +
  geom_label(data = pca_arrows, aes(label = variable), size = 3, alpha = 0.8) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = pal) +
  guides(colour = guide_legend(nrow = 2)) +
  labs(title = "Households on the first two components",
       x = "PC1: Shopping activity and brand variety",
       y = "PC2: Loyal bulk buying versus promotion seeking", colour = NULL)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-pca-segments
#| tbl-cap: "Mean component score of each segment, and the share of each component's variation explained by segment membership."

# Mean score per segment, and R squared of each component's scores on segment
seg_means <- pca_scores |>
  group_by(segment) |>
  summarise(across(all_of(kept_pcs), mean)) |>
  mutate(segment = as.character(segment))

seg_r2 <- map_dbl(kept_pcs, \(pc) summary(lm(reformulate("segment", pc), data = pca_scores))$r.squared) |>
  set_names(kept_pcs)

seg_means |>
  bind_rows(tibble(segment = "Variation explained by segment",
                   PC1 = seg_r2[["PC1"]], PC2 = seg_r2[["PC2"]], PC3 = seg_r2[["PC3"]])) |>
  gt() |>
  fmt_number(all_of(kept_pcs), rows = segment != "Variation explained by segment", decimals = 2) |>
  fmt_percent(all_of(kept_pcs), rows = segment == "Variation explained by segment", decimals = 0) |>
  cols_label(segment = "Segment")
```

```{r}
#| label: pca-segment-values
#| echo: false

sm3 <- \(seg, pc) sprintf("%+.2f", seg_means[[pc]][seg_means$segment == seg])
```

The plot reads like a map of the segments. **Moving right** (PC1) goes from the Light occasional buyers (`r sm3("Light occasional buyers", "PC1")`) to the Heavy multi-brand shoppers (`r sm3("Heavy multi-brand shoppers", "PC1")`), the two ends of shopping activity. **Moving up** (PC2) goes from the Promo-6 buyers at the bottom (`r sm3("Promo-6 buyers", "PC2")`) to the Loyal regular-price buyers (`r sm3("Loyal regular-price buyers", "PC2")`) and Loyal promotion buyers (`r sm3("Loyal promotion buyers", "PC2")`) at the top, the loyalty against deal-seeking axis. The MaxBrShare and PurPromo6 arrows point in opposite directions, so households that are loyal to one brand tend not to rely on promotion 6. PC3, not shown in the plot, is where the **Loyal promotion buyers** stand out (`r sm3("Loyal promotion buyers", "PC3")`), because they are the segment that takes up other promotions.

Segment membership explains `r percent(seg_r2[["PC1"]], accuracy = 1)` of the variation in PC1, `r percent(seg_r2[["PC2"]], accuracy = 1)` in PC2 and `r percent(seg_r2[["PC3"]], accuracy = 1)` in PC3. **The PCA and the clustering therefore tell the same story from two directions:** the clustering finds the groups, and the components name the three dimensions on which they differ, which are activity, loyalty against promotion 6, and response to other promotions.

## What PCA gives up

PCA kept `r round(cum_keep, 1)`% of the information, so `r round(100 - cum_keep, 1)`% of the variation between households is set aside. Three further limits matter for a client:

- **Components are harder to explain than the original variables.** "Shopping activity and brand variety" is a weighted mix of several variables, and a manager may find "number of transactions" easier to act on. This is why the segments in Question 2 were described with the original variables.
- **PCA only finds straight-line relationships, and is pulled by extreme values.** The skew correction and standardisation in @sec-prep reduce this, but a curved pattern, or one driven by a small group of heavy promotion users, can be missed or exaggerated.
- **It cannot compress variables that do not overlap.** `r loner$variable` was nearly unrelated to the others, so it needed a component to itself. When most variables are unrelated, PCA saves little; it is most useful when many variables measure a few underlying ideas.
